title: Rule of use — Scripture / common Schools; creation not apt as praedestinatio-effect
source_text: XXXVI. In hoc autem negotio & aliis similibus haec regula videtur tenenda, nimirum, ut quum agitur de vocum significatione, sequamur, si fieri potest, Scripturae usum, aut saltem non aliter eas accipiamus, quam in Scholis Christianis communiter accipi solent. Itaque cum praedestinatio a communi providentia in Scholis distingui soleat, & communiter ad illam referantur dona gratiae, ad hanc vero naturae bona, minus convenienter creatio poni videtur inter effectus praedestinationis, & consequenter ejus objectum constitui homo nondum a Deo condendus, sed simpliciter creabilis. Nimiumque ampliant vocem praedestinationis, qui sub ea comprehendunt decretum ipsum de homine creando, & lapsu ejus permittendo.
pass_a_gloss: But in this business and in others like it this rule seems to be held: namely that when it is a question of the signification of words, we should follow, if it can be done, the use of Scripture, or at least not take them otherwise than they are commonly taken in the Christian Schools. And so since praedestinatio is wont to be distinguished from common providence in the Schools, and the gifts of grace are commonly referred to the former, but the goods of nature to the latter, creation seems less fittingly placed among the effects of predestination, and consequently its object constituted as man not yet to be created by God, but simply creatable. And those enlarge the word praedestinatio too much who under it comprehend the very decree of creating man and of permitting his fall.
pass_b_english: Rule: follow Scripture’s use of the words, or at least common School use.
Schools distinguish praedestinatio from common providence (grace-gifts vs nature-goods).
Creation less apt as an effect of praedestinatio; object not simply creatable man.
Those who fold create-and-permit-fall under praedestinatio enlarge the word too much.
